turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Brendan? In you come. I put you on the machine on the way past, blood pressure was 138 over 82 and the pulse was 76. Doctor Walsh has your GP's letter about the cough.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, thanks. It's not an emergency or anything, I just can't shake this cough, and the wife said I was to stop putting it off.
[SEG0003] person_3 (DOCTOR): Sit yourself down, Brendan. I'll hear it from you rather than the letter. How long have you had the cough?

[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, solid. It came on the back of a dose of the flu. I was rotten for about a week, fever and aches and the whole production, and then that faded and the cough just... stayed.
[SEG0005] person_3 (DOCTOR): So the fever and the aches themselves have settled?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Settled, yeah. I was back in work after ten days. I'm a stores supervisor in the hardware place in Naas, so there's a fair bit of lifting, and I was able for that once the flu lifted. It's purely the cough now.
[SEG0007] person_3 (DOCTOR): When is the cough at its worst?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Night-time, no question. I'll be just dropping off and up it comes, a dry tickle, and I'm awake for ages. The wife has moved into the spare room, which tells you... anyway. Mornings there's a small amount of white phlegm, and then it's dry the rest of the day.
[SEG0009] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any blood in that phlegm?

[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): No. I have looked, more than once, and there's nothing red in it at all. And it's not a pain in the chest the way a heart pain would be, more a soreness across the front from the hacking itself.
[SEG0011] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any fever now, or proper night sweats, the drenching kind?
[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): The dog has me out the door at half six, rain or shine, down the canal and back, so the mornings are busy. Sorry, I went off on myself there. What was it you asked?
[SEG0013] person_3 (DOCTOR): Fever, or night sweats.
[SEG0014] person_2 (PATIENT): No fever since the flu went. I get a bit clammy when the cough wakes me, but the sheets aren't wet. It's not that drenching kind of sweat.
[SEG0015] person_3 (DOCTOR): And are you breathless with it?
[SEG0016] person_2 (PATIENT): No. The canal walk is grand and the yard is grand. I'm not gasping or anything like that.
[SEG0017] person_3 (DOCTOR): Has your weight or your appetite fallen off?

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): No weight loss. The appetite is as good as ever, the wife still does the full dinner and I clear the plate. I haven't been near a scales, but I don't think I've lost any.
[SEG0019] person_3 (DOCTOR): Have you been abroad lately, or around anyone with tuberculosis?

[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): Abroad, no. I haven't left the country in years, the last holiday was Kerry and that was before Covid. TB, no, I don't know a soul with that. My brother was in Spain in May, but that's his holiday, not mine, I wasn't with him.
[SEG0021] person_3 (DOCTOR): What medicines are you on, including anything from the chemist?

[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): Ramipril five milligrams, one in the morning, for the blood pressure, and I'm on that five years. The GP gave me clarithromycin, five hundred milligrams twice a day for five days, and I finished that about two weeks ago, it did nothing for the cough. At night I take ten mils of Benylin dry cough from the chemist, just to get over.
[SEG0023] person_3 (DOCTOR): Any allergies I should know about before I...

[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Penicillin. I came out in a rash all over when I was seventeen, and they told me not to take it again, so the GP wouldn't give me the usual antibiotic, that's why it was the clarithromycin. I've steered clear of penicillin ever since.
[SEG0025] person_3 (DOCTOR): Do you smoke, or did you?

[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): Never. My father smoked forty a day and I couldn't stick the smell of it in the house, so I never started. I take a pint of a Saturday and that's the height of it, I'm not a drinker.
[SEG0027] person_3 (DOCTOR): Let me have a listen to your chest. Deep breath in... and out. And again for me.

[SEG0028] person_3 (DOCTOR): The lungs are clear, I don't hear any crackles. There's a little wheeze right at the end of the breath, on both sides. Your throat looks ordinary, and there are no glands up in the neck.
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Is the wheeze a bad sign? I have noticed a bit of a whistle at night when I'm lying down, I was going to mention that and then I forgot, the way you do.

[SEG0030] person_3 (DOCTOR): Six weeks on from a flu, worse at night, a bit of phlegm in the morning, and that wheeze. My head runs through a post-viral cough, a twitchy airway, even reflux, and TB does cross my mind when a cough drags on like this. I'm not naming any of those as the cause. I want to see a chest x-ray before I commit to a thing.

[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): The x-ray, do I keep the jumper on or... oh, actually, the trousers. I said I hadn't lost weight, but I've gone in a notch on the belt and the waist is loose, I only copped it getting dressed this week. So I have lost a bit, I was wrong earlier.
[SEG0032] person_3 (DOCTOR): That detail matters, and we'll hold it alongside the film. I'm still not putting a name on this.

[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): And listen, I said no TB, and that's true as far as contact goes, I haven't been near anyone with it. My sister Niamh rang last week going on about our cousin Declan down in Limerick, he was in the hospital with a bad chest and she has it in her head that it was TB. I haven't laid eyes on Declan since a wedding in twenty nineteen, so I wouldn't call that contact.

[SEG0034] person_3 (DOCTOR): So a cousin with a chest illness your sister thinks was tuberculosis, and no contact yourself. I'm still not calling this TB, or calling it anything else. The picture has to come first.

[SEG0035] person_3 (DOCTOR): I'll order a chest x-ray, today if they can fit you in. Keep taking the ramipril as you are, and the Benylin at night is fine if it helps you sleep. I won't be starting any new tablet until we've seen the film.

[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): And if it's something bad on the x-ray, what then? The wife will ask me the minute I get in the door, she has herself half convinced it's desperate, and I keep telling her it's probably nothing.

[SEG0037] person_3 (DOCTOR): Then we deal with whatever the picture shows, not with a guess from me today. If you cough up blood, or you become properly breathless, or a fever comes back, don't wait on the appointment, go to the emergency department or the on-call GP. I'll see you back here in two weeks with the result.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Two weeks, grand. I'll tell the wife, she'll be glad someone is actually looking at it instead of us arguing over it at the kitchen table.
[SEG0039] person_1 (CLINICAL_STAFF): Radiology can take him at half two, so I'll book the chest x-ray and the two-week review on the way out.

spec.situation: Cough for six weeks after flu; worse at night; patient says no weight loss, then says clothes are loose; recent travel or TB contact denied by patient but a family member recalls a cousin's illness; doctor orders chest X-ray, avoids naming a cause.
features: interruptions_trailing_off: people interrupt each other, trail off, or the answer comes two turns after the question.

doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.

bad.reason: White phlegm and small amount are stated; 'every morning' is not explicitly stated.
bad.text: White phlegm in the morning (category=respiratory, status=present, severity=small amount, frequency=every morning, temporality=current, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: Flu with fever/aches for about a week is supported; 'about a week before the cough' is wrong.
bad.text: Flu (category=constitutional, status=resolved, duration=approximately 1 week, onset=about a week before the cough, temporality=resolved, associated_symptoms=fever; aches, reported_by=patient, certainty=certain)

bad.reason: He denies heart-type chest pain but reports chest soreness from coughing, so absolute absence of chest pain is wrong.

omissions.text: The cough is described as a dry tickle at night, with the rest of the day mostly dry apart from a small amount of white phlegm in the mornings.
The doctor documented the lungs as clear overall, not just absence of crackles.
The patient said the chest soreness was not cardiac-type chest pain ('not a pain in the chest the way a heart pain would be'), only soreness across the front from coughing.
The patient had no fever since the flu resolved and was back to work after 10 days once the flu lifted.
Clarithromycin was finished about two weeks ago and the patient said it did nothing for the cough.
Penicillin allergy detail is more specific: he developed a rash all over at age 17 and was told not to take penicillin again.

Although there was a family report of a cousin possibly having TB, the patient clarified he has had no contact with that cousin since a wedding in 2019, so this does not represent TB exposure/contact.

The doctor discussed differential possibilities without committing to a diagnosis: post-viral cough, a twitchy airway, reflux, and tuberculosis were considered, but he explicitly said he was not naming any of them as the cause before the chest X-ray.
